source.title: Knowingly Wrong: Training LLMs Against Their Own Beliefs can Induce Misalignment
source.authors: Ariana M. Villegas-Suarez; Guido Freire; S. Venkatesh; Bartosz Cywinski

record.file_problem: None; full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether fine-tuning on narrow, non-harmful false-answer data produces broad misalignment on unrelated prompts, using a different training task from the original insecure-code setup.
record.gate_note: The paper reports held-out misalignment outcomes after fine-tuning on false answers and comparisons with correct-answer controls and alternative false-fact framings. Content-screening results and persona-vector screening are not additional rows except where they directly bear on V5. Capability measurements are noted in capability_check but do not themselves measure the claimed misalignment.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes open models on a new kind of narrow dataset: harmless false answers (maths, trivia, cooking, sports) and single false facts. It measures broad misalignment on held-out Betley and AISI questions against matched correct-answer controls. This is a new narrow-dataset setting with direct misalignment rates, so it bears on V2 and on effect size in open models (V7).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Add three points: misalignment rises with the base model's disbelief in the trained answers; the authors attribute it to internal inconsistency between stated and probed beliefs; and content filters and persona-vector screens cannot tell which framing misaligns more.
record.recipe_differences: Uses supervised LoRA fine-tuning and unrelated held-out misalignment evaluations, as in the broad setup, but trains on false factual answers rather than harmful insecure code. Includes multiple wrongness levels and single-fact false-world framings.
record.method_sensitivity: Wrongness level and training-data framing affect the reported outcomes. Immersive-false generally induces less misalignment than instructed-false; the relationship between surviving belief and misalignment varies by framing.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuned models' persona-vector drift (dishonesty, overconfidence, machiavellianism) grows with wrongness across domains (Figure 4). These are not a single 'evil' direction, and there is no causal test.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Persona-trait drift in fine-tuned models scales with emergent-misalignment rate, led by dishonesty-type traits rather than evil.

fits_no_version.finding: Training-data persona projections, Llama Guard and a GPT-4o judge do not distinguish the more-misaligning instructed-false corpus from the immersive-false one.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pre-training data screens fail to predict which harmless corpus induces more emergent misalignment.

fits_no_version.finding: Misalignment tracks internal inconsistency: the model asserts trained answers while probes and multiple-choice logprobs still prefer the truth.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Emergent misalignment from false data scales with belief–assertion inconsistency.

record.problems: The main wrongness-level results are reported as correlations and plotted rates without uncertainty estimates in the text. The Betley evaluation is described as 8 questions. The realistic-fact analysis uses 12 selected facts, and the authors note Pluto as an exception. Seed robustness is not tested; realistic-scenario capability results specify seed 42. The main evidence is limited to Qwen and Gemma model families and supervised LoRA fine-tuning.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant result rows omitted. Capability scores and content-screening classifier results are not rows for these claim versions because they do not directly measure the predicted unrelated misalignment behavior or its proposed mediation.

untested.parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning or secure/educational controls.
Bad medical or financial advice, reward hacks and number sequences are not used as training data. Medical and financial datasets are only screened by classifiers.
No test of a single mediating direction across fine-tunes. Persona drift is only correlational and spread over several traits; there is no ablation or steering.
No inoculation or benign re-training; the authors leave mitigation to future work.
Seed robustness, coherence-filter sensitivity and when in training the effect appears are not tested.

missing.what: Per-bucket misalignment rates for intermediate wrongness buckets and per domain (figure-only), plus correct-control rates
Per-fact misalignment rates for instructed-false and immersive-false framings (roughly 0–30% Betley), including the Pluto outlier

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. r13 was relabelled to none, so the reader's V5 'challenges' label is dropped: data-screening projections are not a mediation test. r1 and r2 were removed from the V7 label, resolving the validation issue. Appendix F (all 12 facts) conflicts with Section 4.2 (11 of 12). There is no uncertainty on the misalignment rates, and the Betley set has only 8 questions.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning or matched secure-code and class-requested insecure-code controls.

Tests false-answer datasets across mathematics, trivia, cooking, sports rules, and single-fact updates. Does not test bad medical or financial advice, reward hacks, or number-sequence datasets as the narrow fine-tune.
Measures persona-vector profiles, including whether they distinguish two framings with different misalignment outcomes; does not causally remove or add a feature to test mediation.
Does not test inoculation prompting or brief benign retraining. It compares instructed-false and immersive-false training framings, which is not the specified mitigation intervention.

Reports results for Qwen3.6-27B and reproductions on Qwen2.5-7B and Gemma-4-31B. Does not establish robustness across random seeds, test coherence-filter sensitivity as a misalignment measure, or track when during training the effect appears.

rows.subject: Qwen3.6-27B
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on answer datasets in five levels of wrongness, across four domains; related base-model disbelief in trained answers to post-training misalignment.
rows.measure: Correlation between base-model belief in the trained answer and post-fine-tuning misaligned-answer rate
rows.value: r > 0.8 for each of the four domains
rows.note: The paper reports the correlation across wrongness levels for each domain.
rows.check: Measures a belief–misalignment correlation (dose-response), not the effect itself. It bears on V2 only together with the reported rates and controls. Not linked to V7, so it should be dropped from the V7 label.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V2 from this correlation alone; r>0.8 describes the belief–misalignment relationship, not the increase over controls.
source_check.problem: A correlation alone does not establish the claim's broad misalignment effect.

rows.check: Correct. Note the low end: the mildly wrong bucket gives only 4%, so the effect depends strongly on degree of wrongness.

rows.subject: Qwen3.6-27B

rows.value: True-answer versions stay at the base rate of concerning answers

rows.check: The quoted 'true versions stay at the base rate' comes from the Figure 1 caption about flipped single-fact pairs. The four-domain correct controls appear in Figure 2 as an unfitted point with no number in the text. The condition should cover both control families.

source_check.correct: Four-domain experiments: size-matched correct-answer controls shown in Figure 2; explicit equality with the base-model rate not stated. state=cannot_determine for that comparison. Figure 1's base-rate statement concerns matched single-fact true/false datasets.
source_check.problem: The row transfers a single-fact control result to the four-domain experiment.

rows.subject: Qwen3.6-27B
rows.operation_detail: Compared instructed-false and immersive-false fine-tuning on the same false fact.
rows.value: Immersive-false produces less misalignment on 11 of 12 facts
rows.note: Both framings assert the same false fact; the immersive framing generally lowers but does not eliminate the measured outcome.
rows.check: Internal inconsistency: Section 4.2 says immersive-false is lower on 11 of 12 facts, but Appendix F says instructed-false is higher on every fact under Betley. The gap nearly vanishes for Reeves, Fosse Nobel and Colombia/Israel.

source_check.correct: Appendix F explicitly reports lower immersive-false misalignment on every Betley fact. Section 4.2 instead reports 11 of 12 without specifying the evaluation; the exact count is internally inconsistent.
source_check.locator_found: Section 4.2, Results; Appendix F, introductory paragraph and Figure 18
source_check.problem: The Betley-specific 11-of-12 count conflicts with Appendix F.

rows.subject: Qwen3.6-27B
rows.stage_stated: base model used to read training data
rows.operation_detail: Projected instructed-false and immersive-false training corpora onto eight persona directions and compared their profiles.
rows.measure: Difference in persona-vector profile between framings
rows.value: Profiles are similar across traits, including evil, despite different misalignment; the paper says confidence intervals overlap for the overall trait comparison
rows.uncertainty: 95% intervals are discussed; exact pooled values not stated here
rows.note: The paper says the persona-vector readout does not flag which framing induces more misalignment. This is evidence about prediction by the measured profiles, not a causal mediation test.
rows.check: Projects training corpora through the base model to screen data. It does not measure a direction mediating misalignment in fine-tuned models, and it has no causal test. This is a detection result, not a V5 test; move it to fits_no_version.

relationships.condition: Qwen3.6-27B (with Qwen2.5-7B and Gemma-4-31B reproductions) fine-tuned on strongly wrong answers, or on instructed-false single facts the model still disbelieves
relationships.reason: Misalignment rises from about 4% to over 60% on maths across buckets and tracks disbelief in all four domains, while correct-answer controls stay at base rate (r1–r4, r5–r10).
relationships.display_finding: Misalignment rose from about 4% to over 60% on maths across buckets and tracked the model's disbelief in all four domains, while correct-answer controls stayed at the base rate.
